    Navigator: seven lenses on school mathematics

    Words: 1223

    The blocks of the course are the vertical: from number to space. The lenses are the horizontal: one question put to all the blocks at once.

    Main idea of the navigator #

    Each block teaches its own laws. The navigator shows that these laws share a structure: the same language of notation, a few root laws from which the rest is derived, the same kind of limits and the same traps in the wording of tasks. Whoever sees this structure does not have to memorise mathematics block by block: it comes together as one system.

    1 · Language and notation #

    Mathematics writes briefly, and every sign in the notation matters. −22-2^2 and (−2)2(-2)^2 are different numbers, because the brackets change what the power applies to. f(x+2)f(x + 2) and f(x)+2f(x) + 2 are different functions. A square or a round bracket in an interval decides whether the endpoint is included. Most «careless» NMT mistakes are not carelessness but reading the notation by eye. The skill is simple: before an operation, ask what exactly each sign applies to. The other side of the language is a definition read as a question: the logarithm is «to what power», the root is «what gives this in a power», absolute value is «how far from zero». A definition read as a question points to its own limits.

    Related blocks of the course: 1 · Number and operations, 5 · Function and sequence, 6 · Power, root, logarithm.

    2 · Laws #

    The laws from which school algebra is derived are few. The distributive law gives all the formulas of short multiplication, completing the square, the quadratic formula and the vertex of a parabola. The power law am·an=am+na^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n} gives the properties of roots and logarithms. The law of the part, «part = whole × share», gives percentages, proportions and mixture problems. In geometry such a root is Pythagoras' theorem: from it come the distance between points, the equation of a circle and of a sphere, the diagonal of a cuboid, the basic trigonometric identity, and from its generalisation the cosine rule and the scalar product. The NMT reference sheet has many formulas but only a few roots: whoever knows the roots can rebuild any formula and see when it fits.

    Related blocks of the course: 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent, 3 · Algebraic expressions, 6 · Power, root, logarithm, 11 · Measurement in the plane, 12 · Coordinates and vectors.

    3 · Proof #

    No proofs are written at the NMT, but a proof is what ties a law to memory. Most school proofs are shorter than a paragraph: the test for divisibility by 9 holds because 10=9+110 = 9 + 1; the angle sum of a triangle is a line parallel to the base; Pythagoras is a square made of four triangles; the volume of a pyramid is a cube cut into three pyramids; Newton - Leibniz is a strip of area of width h. A good proof does not only convince but also shows the limits of the law: the proof of the zero product divides by a and so explains at once why you cannot divide by zero; the proof of the quadratic formula shows where the discriminant comes from and why there are no roots when it is negative.

    Related blocks of the course: 1 · Number and operations, 4 · Equations and inequalities, 8 · Derivative and integral, 10 · Figures in the plane, 13 · Space.

    4 · Applicability #

    Each section answers its own question, and an NMT task is a question dressed up as a story. «What part, how many percent» is block 2. «For which x» is an equation, block 4. «How does it depend» is a function, block 5. «How many times does it grow at each step» is the exponential function and the logarithm, block 6. «What repeats» is trigonometry, block 7. «How fast does it change, where is it largest, how much has accumulated» is the derivative and the integral, block 8. «How many options, what are the chances» is block 9. Recognising the question behind the story is the first step of a solution, and that is exactly what the reverse move in each block trains: a task without a hint, where you name the law.

    Related blocks of the course: 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent, 4 · Equations and inequalities, 5 · Function and sequence, 8 · Derivative and integral, 9 · Combinatorics, probability, statistics.

    5 · Limits #

    The limits of the laws share an origin: almost all of them are division by zero, an even root of a negative number or the logarithm of a non-positive one. Hence the domain in equations, the punctured points when fractions are cancelled, extraneous roots after squaring, the condition |a|≤1|a| \leq 1 for sine and cosine. The second family of limits is the sign: multiplying an inequality by a negative number, a logarithm base between 0 and 1, an obtuse angle in the cosine rule. The third is scale: area grows as the square, volume as the cube, successive percentages multiply. Whoever knows these three families checks an answer not by solving again but with a question: have I stepped over one of the limits?

    Related blocks of the course: 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent, 3 · Algebraic expressions, 4 · Equations and inequalities, 6 · Power, root, logarithm, 7 · Trigonometry, 13 · Space.

    6 · Links between sections #

    The blocks grow out of one another. Number (1) gives the laws of operations; ratio (2) gives the share; expressions (3) write the laws with letters; equations (4) look for where an identity stops being an identity; a function (5) looks at an equation as a whole; power and logarithm (6) are three questions to one equality; the derivative (8) measures how fast a function changes. Trigonometry (7) grows out of similar triangles (10), and coordinates (12) join geometry to algebra: distance is Pythagoras (11), the equation of a circle is an equation from block 4, the scalar product is the cosine rule. Space (13) comes down to the plane. So before the NMT it is worth revising not «topics» but chains: a forgotten law is rebuilt from the one before it.

    Related blocks of the course: 1 · Number and operations, 5 · Function and sequence, 7 · Trigonometry, 10 · Figures in the plane, 12 · Coordinates and vectors.

    7 · Traps in NMT wording #

    The wrong options in choice tasks are not random numbers. They are the results of typical blind moves: percentages added instead of multiplied, a minus forgotten in the vertex formula, the sum of the legs instead of the hypotenuse, the lateral surface instead of the total one, a root that did not pass the domain check. So an answer that matches one of the options proves nothing. Other traps hide in words: «by how many percent more» and «what percentage is»; «lateral» and «total»; «the greatest value on a segment» (then the endpoints are checked too); «the point of maximum» (they ask for x, not the value of the function); «if there are several roots, write their sum» (often a sign that one root is extraneous). Almost all the hardest tasks of NMT 2026 stand on one of these traps.

    Related blocks of the course: 2 · Ratio, proportion, percent, 5 · Function and sequence, 6 · Power, root, logarithm, 8 · Derivative and integral, 13 · Space.
